claim: The camera survey yielded 786 detections of apex predators over 21,430 trap-nights throughout the West African study system.
source: Our camera survey yielded 786 and 10,325 detections of apex predators and ungulates, respectively, over 21,430 trap-nights throughout our West African study system (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the number of apex predator detections and trap-nights from their camera survey.

claim: The camera survey yielded 10,325 detections of ungulates over 21,430 trap-nights throughout the West African study system.
source: Our camera survey yielded 786 and 10,325 detections of apex predators and ungulates, respectively, over 21,430 trap-nights throughout our West African study system (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the number of ungulate detections from their camera survey.

claim: Spotted hyenas are the dominant predator in the system with six times more detections than either African lions or leopards.
source: Spotted hyenas are the dominant predator in the system with six times more detections than either African lions or leopards.
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative detection rates among the three predator species from their camera survey data.

claim: Warthog, reedbuck, and bushbuck were the most commonly observed ungulates, each detected over 1000 times.
source: Warthog, reedbuck, and bushbuck were the most commonly observed ungulates, each detected over 1000 times.
evidence: The manuscript reports detection frequencies for specific ungulate species from their camera survey.

claim: 350 detections of humans were obtained in 69 out of 204 surveyed 10-km2 grid cells.
source: We obtained 350 detections of humans in 69 out of 204 surveyed 10-km2 grid cells, leading to a naive human occupancy of 0.34.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of human detections and the number of grid cells where humans were detected.

claim: The naive human occupancy was 0.34.
source: We obtained 350 detections of humans in 69 out of 204 surveyed 10-km2 grid cells, leading to a naive human occupancy of 0.34.
evidence: The manuscript reports the calculated naive occupancy value based on detection data.

claim: Model selection resulted in four competing top models (ΔAICc < 2) for human occupancy.
source: Accounting for imperfect detection, model selection resulted in four competing top models (ΔAICc < 2) for human occupancy (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of their model selection process for human occupancy.

claim: Detection of humans primarily varied among years and sites and was higher in non-savanna habitat.
source: Detection of humans primarily varied among years and sites and was higher in non-savanna habitat (top model goodness-of-fit p-value = 0.327).
evidence: The manuscript reports the factors that influenced human detection based on their occupancy modeling results.

claim: The top model for human occupancy had a goodness-of-fit p-value of 0.327.
source: Detection of humans primarily varied among years and sites and was higher in non-savanna habitat (top model goodness-of-fit p-value = 0.327).
evidence: The manuscript reports the goodness-of-fit statistic for their top occupancy model.

claim: 108 of 204 grid cells were designated as having high human use (occupancy > 0.54).
source: Using the mean value of occupancy as a pressure threshold, we designated 108 of 204 grid cells as having high human use (occupancy > 0.54).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of grid cells classified as high human use based on their threshold criterion.

claim: Humans exhibited mostly diurnal activity with 80.3% of detections occurring between sunrise and sunset.
source: Humans exhibited mostly diurnal activity with 80.3% of detections occurring between sunrise and sunset (Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of human detections during daylight hours, with reference to Figure 2c showing the temporal distribution.

claim: Carnivores showed significantly different diel activity patterns between low and high human use (p-value=0.017).
source: Carnivores and ungulates showed significantly different diel activity patterns between low and high human use (carnivores p-value=0.017; ungulates p-value<0.001; Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical test result for differences in carnivore diel activity patterns between human use levels.

claim: Ungulates showed significantly different diel activity patterns between low and high human use (p-value<0.001).
source: Carnivores and ungulates showed significantly different diel activity patterns between low and high human use (carnivores p-value=0.017; ungulates p-value<0.001; Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical test result for differences in ungulate diel activity patterns between human use levels.

claim: Over two-thirds (10 out of 14) of the mammal species in the study exhibited significant differences in their diel activity patterns in response to human presence.
source: Over two-thirds (10 out of 14) of the mammal species in the study exhibited significant differences in their diel activity patterns in response to human presence (African leopards, spotted hyenas, and eight ungulates; Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion and specific species showing significant diel activity differences.

claim: African leopards exhibited significant differences in their diel activity patterns in response to human presence.
source: Over two-thirds (10 out of 14) of the mammal species in the study exhibited significant differences in their diel activity patterns in response to human presence (African leopards, spotted hyenas, and eight ungulates; Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript lists African leopards as one of the species showing significant diel activity differences.

claim: Spotted hyenas exhibited significant differences in their diel activity patterns in response to human presence.
source: Over two-thirds (10 out of 14) of the mammal species in the study exhibited significant differences in their diel activity patterns in response to human presence (African leopards, spotted hyenas, and eight ungulates; Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript lists spotted hyenas as one of the species showing significant diel activity differences.

claim: Eight ungulate species exhibited significant differences in their diel activity patterns in response to human presence.
source: Over two-thirds (10 out of 14) of the mammal species in the study exhibited significant differences in their diel activity patterns in response to human presence (African leopards, spotted hyenas, and eight ungulates; Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports that eight ungulate species showed significant diel activity differences.

claim: Ungulates overall were 7.1% (95% CI ± 1.7%) more active at night in high human areas.
source: Ungulates overall were 7.1% (95% CI ± 1.7%) more active at night in high human areas, while carnivores showed a slight but non-significant increase in night-time activity of 3.9% (±5.7%).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage increase in nocturnal activity for ungulates with confidence intervals.

claim: Carnivores showed a slight but non-significant increase in night-time activity of 3.9% (±5.7%) in high human areas.
source: Ungulates overall were 7.1% (95% CI ± 1.7%) more active at night in high human areas, while carnivores showed a slight but non-significant increase in night-time activity of 3.9% (±5.7%).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage increase in nocturnal activity for carnivores with confidence intervals and notes it is non-significant.

claim: Reedbuck showed significantly higher nocturnal activity (+12.3 ± 4.8%) with high human use.
source: Specifically, we observed significantly higher nocturnal activity with high human use for reedbuck (+12.3 ± 4.8%), duiker (+7.4 ± 4.4%), bushbuck (+6.9 ± 3.6%), and warthog (+4.5 ± 1.9%); and significant decreases for kob (−5.3 ± 4.2%) and aardvark (−15.0 ± 8.1%; Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific change in nocturnal activity for reedbuck with confidence intervals.

claim: Duiker showed significantly higher nocturnal activity (+7.4 ± 4.4%) with high human use.
source: Specifically, we observed significantly higher nocturnal activity with high human use for reedbuck (+12.3 ± 4.8%), duiker (+7.4 ± 4.4%), bushbuck (+6.9 ± 3.6%), and warthog (+4.5 ± 1.9%); and significant decreases for kob (−5.3 ± 4.2%) and aardvark (−15.0 ± 8.1%; Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific change in nocturnal activity for duiker with confidence intervals.

claim: Bushbuck showed significantly higher nocturnal activity (+6.9 ± 3.6%) with high human use.
source: Specifically, we observed significantly higher nocturnal activity with high human use for reedbuck (+12.3 ± 4.8%), duiker (+7.4 ± 4.4%), bushbuck (+6.9 ± 3.6%), and warthog (+4.5 ± 1.9%); and significant decreases for kob (−5.3 ± 4.2%) and aardvark (−15.0 ± 8.1%; Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific change in nocturnal activity for bushbuck with confidence intervals.

claim: Warthog showed significantly higher nocturnal activity (+4.5 ± 1.9%) with high human use.
source: Specifically, we observed significantly higher nocturnal activity with high human use for reedbuck (+12.3 ± 4.8%), duiker (+7.4 ± 4.4%), bushbuck (+6.9 ± 3.6%), and warthog (+4.5 ± 1.9%); and significant decreases for kob (−5.3 ± 4.2%) and aardvark (−15.0 ± 8.1%; Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific change in nocturnal activity for warthog with confidence intervals.

claim: Kob showed a significant decrease in nocturnal activity (−5.3 ± 4.2%) with high human use.
source: Specifically, we observed significantly higher nocturnal activity with high human use for reedbuck (+12.3 ± 4.8%), duiker (+7.4 ± 4.4%), bushbuck (+6.9 ± 3.6%), and warthog (+4.5 ± 1.9%); and significant decreases for kob (−5.3 ± 4.2%) and aardvark (−15.0 ± 8.1%; Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific change in nocturnal activity for kob with confidence intervals.

claim: Aardvark showed a significant decrease in nocturnal activity (−15.0 ± 8.1%) with high human use.
source: Specifically, we observed significantly higher nocturnal activity with high human use for reedbuck (+12.3 ± 4.8%), duiker (+7.4 ± 4.4%), bushbuck (+6.9 ± 3.6%), and warthog (+4.5 ± 1.9%); and significant decreases for kob (−5.3 ± 4.2%) and aardvark (−15.0 ± 8.1%; Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific change in nocturnal activity for aardvark with confidence intervals.

claim: Five ungulate species showed no significant differences in nocturnality in response to human presence.
source: In contrast, five ungulate species and all three carnivores showed no significant differences in nocturnality.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of ungulate species that did not show significant changes in nocturnal activity.

claim: All three carnivores showed no significant differences in nocturnality in response to human presence.
source: In contrast, five ungulate species and all three carnivores showed no significant differences in nocturnality.
evidence: The manuscript reports that none of the three carnivore species showed significant changes in nocturnal activity.

claim: Increasing or decreasing the human occupancy threshold by ±0.1 did not alter the interpretation of species' differences in diel activity for most species.
source: After testing the sensitivity of our results to the human occupancy threshold selected, we found that increasing or decreasing the low vs. high human occupancy threshold by ±0.1 did not alter our interpretation of species' differences in diel activity (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of their sensitivity analysis for the human occupancy threshold.

claim: Reducing the human occupancy threshold from 0.54 to 0.44 resulted in detecting significance for African leopard and roan antelope.
source: The only change we observed was detecting significance when reducing the threshold from 0.54 to 0.44 for two species: African leopard and roan antelope.
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific changes observed in the sensitivity analysis.

claim: Differences in diel activity among species did not result in significant differences in individual predators' temporal overlap (Δ) with prey when prey species were aggregated.
source: Differences in diel activity among species did not result in significant differences in individual predators' temporal overlap (Δ) with prey when we aggregated their prey species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of their temporal overlap analysis for aggregated prey.

claim: All three species to which predator access increased significantly also exhibited increased night-time activity as a human avoidance strategy.
source: All three species to which predator access increased significantly also exhibited increased night-time activity as a human avoidance strategy.
evidence: The manuscript reports the relationship between increased predator access and increased nocturnal activity in prey species.

claim: Kob was less active at night in high human areas and experienced lower overlap with African lions and spotted hyenas.
source: In contrast, kob was less active at night in high human areas and experienced lower overlap with African lions and spotted hyenas (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the relationship between decreased nocturnal activity in kob and decreased predator overlap.

claim: All three apex predators showed comparable differences in access to all prey between human use levels.
source: All three apex predators showed comparable differences in access to all prey between human use levels (Figure 5b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the overall pattern of prey access changes across all three predators.

claim: Leopards showed a differential response to human presence (-4.6 ± 19.1% change in nocturnality) compared to African lions (+11.9 ± 16.3%) and spotted hyenas (+3.7 ± 6.5%).
source: We suspect this is due to leopards' differential response to human presence (-4.6 ± 19.1% change in nocturnality) compared to African lions (+11.9 ± 16.3%) and spotted hyenas (+3.7 ± 6.5%; Figure 4), although these differences are non-significant.
evidence: The manuscript reports the changes in nocturnality for all three predators with confidence intervals.

claim: Human presence increased the variation in species-specific prey accessibility (PAUC estimates) for African lions (Fligner-Killeen test, p-value=0.03).
source: Although overlap with total available prey did not differ for any predator, human presence increased the variation in species-specific prey accessibility (PAUC estimates) for African lions (Fligner-Killeen test, p-value=0.03), indicating lower diversity of available prey and therefore more access to certain prey species compared to others where human presence was high (Figure 5b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical test result for variation in prey accessibility for lions.

claim: African leopards showed no significant differences in access variability as a response to humans.
source: African leopards and spotted hyenas showed no significant differences in access variability as a response to humans.
evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of significant differences in prey access variability for leopards.

claim: Spotted hyenas showed no significant differences in access variability as a response to humans.
source: African leopards and spotted hyenas showed no significant differences in access variability as a response to humans.
evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of significant differences in prey access variability for spotted hyenas.

claim: The study was conducted in the W-Arly-Pendjari (WAP) protected area complex that spans 26,515 km2 in the transboundary region of Burkina Faso, Niger, and Benin (0°E-3° E, 10°N-13°N).
source: We conducted our study in the W-Arly-Pendjari (WAP) protected area complex that spans 26,515 km2 in the transboundary region of Burkina Faso, Niger, and Benin (0°E-3° E, 10°N-13°N; Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the geographic location and size of the study area.

claim: The WAP complex contains 5 national parks (54% of total area), 14 hunting concessions (40%), and 1 faunal reserve (6%).
source: The complex contains 5 national parks (54% of total area), 14 hunting concessions (40%), and 1 faunal reserve (6%).
evidence: The manuscript describes the composition of protected areas within the WAP complex.

claim: The study area within WAP comprised three national parks and 11 hunting concessions in Burkina Faso and Niger across ca. 13,100 km2.
source: Our study area within WAP comprised three national parks and 11 hunting concessions in Burkina Faso and Niger across ca. 13,100 km2 (Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the specific study area within the larger WAP complex.

claim: Trophy hunting of many ungulate species and African lions (Panthera leo) is permitted in hunting concessions.
source: Trophy hunting of many ungulate species and African lions (Panthera leo) is permitted in hunting concessions, while all hunting is illegal in the national parks and reserves in the complex.
evidence: The manuscript describes the hunting regulations in different parts of the study area.

claim: All hunting is illegal in the national parks and reserves in the WAP complex.
source: Trophy hunting of many ungulate species and African lions (Panthera leo) is permitted in hunting concessions, while all hunting is illegal in the national parks and reserves in the complex.
evidence: The manuscript describes the hunting regulations in different parts of the study area.

claim: Human activities in the park include livestock herding, resource extraction, recreation, and poaching.
source: Other human activities in the park include livestock herding, resource extraction, recreation, and poaching (Sogbohossou et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2015; Harris et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript lists the types of human activities occurring in the study area, supported by citations.

claim: Harris et al., 2019 reported 4 large carnivore species (African lion, African leopard Panthera pardus, spotted hyena Crocuta crocuta, and cheetah Acinonyx jubatus) in the three national parks included in the study area.
source: Recently, Harris et al., 2019 reported 4 large carnivore species (African lion, African leopard Panthera pardus, spotted hyena Crocuta crocuta, and cheetah Acinonyx jubatus) and 17 ungulate species belonging to the superorder Ungulata in the three national parks included in our study area from an extensive camera trap survey.
evidence: The manuscript cites Harris et al., 2019 for the species composition in the study area.

claim: Harris et al., 2019 reported 17 ungulate species belonging to the superorder Ungulata in the three national parks included in the study area.
source: Recently, Harris et al., 2019 reported 4 large carnivore species (African lion, African leopard Panthera pardus, spotted hyena Crocuta crocuta, and cheetah Acinonyx jubatus) and 17 ungulate species belonging to the superorder Ungulata in the three national parks included in our study area from an extensive camera trap survey.
evidence: The manuscript cites Harris et al., 2019 for the species composition in the study area.

claim: Cheetahs were detected only once in the study area.
source: Cheetahs were detected only once, while wild dogs (Lycaon pictus) were not reported in the survey area.
evidence: The manuscript reports the detection frequency for cheetahs.

claim: Wild dogs (Lycaon pictus) were not reported in the survey area.
source: Cheetahs were detected only once, while wild dogs (Lycaon pictus) were not reported in the survey area.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of wild dog detections.

claim: WAP has an arid climate and consists predominantly of Sudanian and Sahel savannas, with savanna accounting for ca. 90% of the habitat cover in the study area.
source: WAP has an arid climate and consists predominantly of Sudanian and Sahel savannas, with savanna accounting for ca. 90% of the habitat cover in the study area (Lamarque, 2004; Mills et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript describes the climate and habitat composition of the study area, supported by citations.

claim: The survey was conducted in the drier northern portion of WAP during the dry season with average monthly rainfall ranging from 0 to 1 mm in February to 42–91 mm in June.
source: We conducted our survey in the drier northern portion of WAP during the dry season with average monthly rainfall ranging from 0 to 1 mm in February to 42–91 mm in June (Fick and Hijmans, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the timing and rainfall conditions during the survey period, supported by a citation.

claim: Evidence suggests that large African herbivores show similar overall temporal activity distributions as seasons change.
source: Although our study design may limit inferences to dry season conditions, evidence suggests that large African herbivores show similar overall temporal activity distributions as seasons change (Owen-Smith et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Owen-Smith et al., 2010 to support the claim about seasonal consistency in herbivore activity patterns.

claim: 238 white-flash and infrared motion-sensor cameras (Reconyx PC800, PC850, PC900) were systematically deployed within 10 × 10 km grid cells across the study area.
source: We systematically deployed 238 white-flash and infrared motion-sensor cameras (Reconyx [Holmen, WI] PC800, PC850, PC900) within 10 × 10 km grid cells across our study area to assess effects of human presence on diel activity within the wildlife community.
evidence: The manuscript describes the camera equipment and deployment design.

claim: A single unbaited camera was placed within 2 km of the centroid in a total of 204 sampled grid cells over three survey seasons from January to June in 2016–2018.
source: A single unbaited camera was placed within 2 km of the centroid in a total of 204 sampled grid cells over three survey seasons from January to June in 2016–2018 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the camera placement protocol and survey timing.

claim: Fifty cameras were deployed in 2016.
source: Fifty cameras were deployed in 2016, 115 cameras in 2017, and 73 cameras in 2018.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 caption reports the number of cameras deployed in 2016.

claim: 115 cameras were deployed in 2017.
source: Fifty cameras were deployed in 2016, 115 cameras in 2017, and 73 cameras in 2018.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 caption reports the number of cameras deployed in 2017.

claim: 73 cameras were deployed in 2018.
source: Fifty cameras were deployed in 2016, 115 cameras in 2017, and 73 cameras in 2018.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 caption reports the number of cameras deployed in 2018.

claim: Species identifications from camera images were validated by two members of the Applied Wildlife Ecology (AWE) Lab at the University of Michigan.
source: Species identifications from camera images were validated by two members of the Applied Wildlife Ecology (AWE) Lab at the University of Michigan.
evidence: The manuscript describes the validation process for species identifications.

claim: False triggers, unidentifiable images, research team, and park staff were excluded from analyses.
source: We excluded false triggers, unidentifiable images, research team, and park staff from analyses.
evidence: The manuscript describes the data filtering criteria.

claim: All remaining human images were combined into a single 'Human' categorization representing a variety of human activities observed in WAP.
source: To ensure robustness in our analyses, we combined all remaining human images into a single 'Human' categorization representing a variety of human activities observed in WAP (e.g. livestock herding, resource gathering, recreation, poaching, and hunting).
evidence: The manuscript describes how human detections were categorized for analysis.

claim: Survey data from all 3 years were aggregated into a single dataset due to limited detections for some species.
source: Due to limited detections for some species, we aggregated survey data from all 3 years into a single dataset.
evidence: The manuscript explains the rationale for aggregating data across years.

claim: Previous work suggests little annual variation in wildlife activity.
source: We accounted for temporal variation in human space use during the subsequent modeling process, and previous work suggests little annual variation in wildlife activity (Mills et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites Mills et al., 2020 to support the claim about annual consistency in wildlife activity.

claim: Independence of species triggers was created using a 30-min quiet period between detection events using the 'camtrapR' package in R 3.5.1.
source: We created independence of species triggers using a 30-min quiet period between detection events using the 'camtrapR' package in R 3.5.1 (http://www.r-project.org) (Niedballa et al., 2016), and we assumed detections to be a random sample of each species' underlying activity distribution (Linkie and Ridout, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript describes the method for ensuring independence of detections, with citations to the software package and methodological reference.

claim: Detections were assumed to be a random sample of each species' underlying activity distribution.
source: We created independence of species triggers using a 30-min quiet period between detection events using the 'camtrapR' package in R 3.5.1 (http://www.r-project.org) (Niedballa et al., 2016), and we assumed detections to be a random sample of each species' underlying activity distribution (Linkie and Ridout, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript states the assumption about detection sampling, with a citation to support this approach.

claim: Single-season, single-species occupancy models were constructed to designate WAP into areas of low and high human use.
source: We constructed single-season, single-species occupancy models to designate WAP into areas of low and high human use.
evidence: The manuscript describes the modeling approach used for human occupancy.

claim: Detection/non-detection data for humans were separated into 2-week observation periods, which were modeled as independent surveys to account for imperfect detection.
source: We separated detection/non-detection data for humans into 2-week observation periods, which were modeled as independent surveys to account for imperfect detection.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal structure of the occupancy modeling approach.

claim: The global detection model included covariates related to survey design and the environment: % savanna habitat (SAV), survey year (YR), trap-nights (TN), camera type (CAM), management type (MGMT), and site (SITE).
source: The global detection model included covariates related to survey design and the environment that we expected to influence the detection of humans: % savanna habitat (SAV), survey year (YR), trap-nights (TN), camera type (CAM), management type (MGMT), and site (i.e. one of 14 individual parks or concessions; SITE).
evidence: The manuscript lists the covariates included in the detection model.

claim: MGMT was a binary variable that distinguished national parks from hunting concessions.
source: MGMT was a binary variable that distinguished national parks from hunting concessions.
evidence: The manuscript defines the MGMT covariate.

claim: Human occupancy was modeled with only grouping variables: MGMT, YR, and SITE.
source: Human occupancy was modeled with only grouping variables: MGMT, YR, and SITE.
evidence: The manuscript lists the covariates included in the occupancy model.

claim: YR was included as a covariate to account for temporal variation in site use or detection, as cells surveyed in multiple years were considered separate sites for the single-season model.
source: We included YR as a covariate to account for temporal variation in site use or detection, as cells surveyed in multiple years were considered separate sites for our single-season model.
evidence: The manuscript explains the rationale for including year as a covariate.

claim: A grid cell surveyed in multiple years could have different levels of occupancy between surveys.
source: A grid cell surveyed in multiple years could, therefore, have different levels of occupancy between surveys.
evidence: The manuscript explains how repeated surveys of the same grid cell were treated in the analysis.

claim: All combinations of detection and occupancy covariates were evaluated using the Akaike information criterion corrected for small sample sizes (AICc).
source: We evaluated the support for all combinations of detection and occupancy covariates using the Akaike information criterion corrected for small sample sizes (AICc).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model selection criterion used.

claim: The top-performing detection and occupancy models were selected as those with ΔAICc <2 compared to the lowest AICc model.
source: We selected the top-performing detection and occupancy models as those with ΔAICc <2 compared to the lowest AICc model.
evidence: The manuscript describes the threshold for selecting top models.

claim: Goodness-of-fit of the top-performing models was assessed using 1000 parametric bootstraps of a χ2 test statistic appropriate for binary data.
source: We assessed goodness-of-fit of the top-performing models using 1000 parametric bootstraps of a χ2 test statistic appropriate for binary data and estimated the ĉ statistic to ensure the data were not over-dispersed (Fiske and Chandler, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the goodness-of-fit assessment method with a citation.

claim: The ĉ statistic was estimated to ensure the data were not over-dispersed.
source: We assessed goodness-of-fit of the top-performing models using 1000 parametric bootstraps of a χ2 test statistic appropriate for binary data and estimated the ĉ statistic to ensure the data were not over-dispersed (Fiske and Chandler, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the use of the ĉ statistic with a citation.

claim: All detection and occupancy models were created using the 'unmarked' package in R.
source: We created all detection and occupancy models using the 'unmarked' package and conducted model selection using the 'MuMIn' package in R (Fiske and Chandler, 2011; Bartoń, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites the software package used for occupancy modeling.

claim: Model selection was conducted using the 'MuMIn' package in R.
source: We created all detection and occupancy models using the 'unmarked' package and conducted model selection using the 'MuMIn' package in R (Fiske and Chandler, 2011; Bartoń, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites the software package used for model selection.

claim: Cell-specific latent occupancy probabilities were extracted from the top-performing occupancy model corrected for imperfect detection.
source: We extracted cell-specific latent occupancy probabilities, representing probabilities of site use by humans because the 10-km2 grid cells do not meet the assumption of closure, from the top-performing (lowest AICc) occupancy model corrected for imperfect detection (MacKenzie et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript describes the extraction of occupancy estimates with a citation to the methodological reference.

claim: The 10-km2 grid cells do not meet the assumption of closure for occupancy modeling.
source: We extracted cell-specific latent occupancy probabilities, representing probabilities of site use by humans because the 10-km2 grid cells do not meet the assumption of closure, from the top-performing (lowest AICc) occupancy model corrected for imperfect detection (MacKenzie et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation of the occupancy modeling approach.

claim: The threshold for human use was delineated using the mean value of human occupancy.
source: We delineated the threshold for human use using the mean value of human occupancy.
evidence: The manuscript describes the method for categorizing human use levels.

claim: The mean occupancy was chosen as the threshold value because of the bimodal distribution of occupancy values and to facilitate comparisons between similar sample sizes of low and high human use grid cells.
source: We chose to use the mean occupancy as the threshold value because of the bimodal distribution of occupancy values and to facilitate comparisons between similar sample sizes of low and high human use grid cells (Figure 2b).
evidence: The manuscript explains the rationale for selecting the mean as the threshold.

claim: The study included 12 ungulate species: savanna buffalo, roan antelope, western hartebeest, waterbuck, Buffon's kob, Bohor reedbuck, bushbuck, aardvark, warthog, oribi, red-flanked duiker, and common duiker.
source: We included 12 ungulate species: savanna buffalo (Syncerus caffer brachyceros), roan antelope (Hippotragus equinus koba), western hartebeest (Alcelaphus buselaphus major), waterbuck (Kobus ellipsiprymnus defassa), Buffon's kob (Kobus kob kob), Bohor reedbuck (Redunca redunca), bushbuck (Tragelaphus sylvaticus), aardvark (Orycteropus afer), warthog (Phacochoerus africanus), oribi (Ourebia ourebi), red-flanked duiker (Cephalophus rufilatus), and common duiker (Sylvicapra grimmia).
evidence: The manuscript lists all ungulate species included in the analysis.

claim: Topi and red-fronted gazelle were excluded from analysis due to few detections (<50).
source: We excluded four ungulate species from analysis in our study: topi (Damaliscus korrigum jimela) and red-fronted gazelle (Eudorcas rufifrons) due to few detections (<50), and elephant (Loxodonta africana) and hippopotamus (Hippopotamus amphibius) due to large body sizes that make them uncommon prey items for large carnivores.
evidence: The manuscript explains the exclusion criteria for certain ungulate species.

claim: Elephant and hippopotamus were excluded from analysis due to large body sizes that make them uncommon prey items for large carnivores.
source: We excluded four ungulate species from analysis in our study: topi (Damaliscus korrigum jimela) and red-fronted gazelle (Eudorcas rufifrons) due to few detections (<50), and elephant (Loxodonta africana) and hippopotamus (Hippopotamus amphibius) due to large body sizes that make them uncommon prey items for large carnivores.
evidence: The manuscript explains the exclusion criteria for certain ungulate species.
